jkText:
Conformity with ISO 18286.1 is maintained through this AI governance workflow, which constitutes the organisation's formal compliance strategy:

1. Classification (Step 3) — Each AI system is classified against the EU AI Act. Applicable articles, organisation role (provider/deployer), and any substantial modification obligations are identified and recorded.

2. Risk Assessment (Step 5) — Legal and regulatory risks (GDPR, IP, copyright, and EU AI Act obligations per applicable articles) are assessed against their attack vectors. Risks linked to non-applicable articles are pre-filtered and documented with the reason.

3. Control Selection (Step 6) — The risk team selects controls to treat each identified risk. Every risk must have at least one control before the assessment can be saved.

4. Compliance Coverage (Step 6, AI Act Compliance Controls view) — The compliance team verifies that every harmonised standard requirement has at least one selected control. Uncovered requirements are surfaced as gaps and addressed by adding compliance-specific controls in consultation with the risk team.

5. Traceability — End-to-end traceability is maintained: AI Act article → harmonised standard requirement → selected control → implementation task → test. Gap detection runs automatically on every view render.

6. Modifications — Where a substantial modification is identified in Step 3, Article 25 obligations are triggered, provider-level Articles 9–17 are added to the applicable articles, and Steps 5 and 6 are completed on the full provider obligations basis.

Completion of this workflow, with all applicable HS requirements covered and no unresolved gaps, constitutes the organisation's compliance record under this standard.
jkObjective: This AI governance workflow (Steps 3–7 and the AI Act Compliance Controls view) constitutes the organisation's formal compliance strategy under ISO 18286.1, providing a repeatable, auditable process for identifying applicable obligations, treating risks, selecting controls, and maintaining ongoing HS traceability.
jkImplementationEvidence: Saved Step 3, Step 8, and Step 9 records for the system under assessment. The AI Act Compliance View showing full HS coverage with zero unresolved gaps serves as the compliance evidence for this control.

jkName: AI Governance Workflow — System Identity and Purpose
jkText:
Conformity with ISO 18286.9 is maintained through Step 2 of this governance workflow:

1. System identification (Step 2) — The AI Tool Use Case request form requires the requestor to name the AI tool, identify its specific version or model where known, and describe the precise task it will perform within the organisation.

2. Intended purpose declaration (Step 2) — The business case requires explicit documentation of what the tool is designed to do in this deployment context, what output it will produce, and how that output will be used.

3. Scope and access duration (Step 2) — The form records whether use is single-instance or ongoing, the access period, and the specific team or individuals who will use the tool, bounding the declared purpose to a defined operational scope.

4. Department Head endorsement (Step 2) — The countersignature confirms that the documented purpose is authorised and represents a legitimate business need, providing a formal attestation of the system's intended role.
jkObjective: Step 2 of the AI governance workflow produces a documented declaration of the AI system's identity, intended purpose, and operational scope, satisfying the system description requirements of ISO 18286.9.
jkImplementationEvidence: Saved Step 2 AI Tool Use Case request form, showing system name, task description, access duration, and Department Head countersignature.

jkText:
Conformity with ISO 18286.2 is maintained through this governance workflow, which establishes clear roles and management responsibilities for AI safety at each stage:

1. Requestor accountability (Steps 1–4) — The requestor must confirm training completion, document the business case with specificity, declare data types, and countersign the AI Tool Use Case form before submission.

2. Department Head sign-off (Step 2) — A countersignature by a Department Head is mandatory before any submission reaches AI Governance Team, establishing direct line management accountability for the use case.

3. AI Governance Team governance (Steps 5–7) — The AI Governance Team holds the risk assessment, control, and verification mandate, providing a dedicated expert function accountable for AI safety governance.

4. DPO responsibility (Step 4) — Where personal data is involved, the DPO leads the DPIA and holds sign-off authority, with a hard stop gate if no lawful basis can be established.

5. AI Change Board authority (Step 8) — Board review is mandatory for Tier 2 and elevated-risk cases, providing a governance layer with documented approval or rejection records.

6. CISO and Steering Committee oversight (Steps 11–12) — The CISO maintains the central inventory and Steering Committee receives ongoing governance reports, completing the management accountability chain.
jkObjective: This AI governance workflow constitutes the organisation's accountability framework under ISO 18286.2, with defined roles and escalation paths from requestor through Department Head, AI Governance Team, DPO, AI Change Board, and CISO/Steering Committee.
jkImplementationEvidence: Saved Step 2 record (AI Tool Use Case request form countersigned by Department Head) and the AI Change Board decision record from Step 11.

jkText:
Conformity with ISO 18286.8 is maintained through this governance workflow, which generates and retains all required documentation at each stage:

1. Request form (Step 2) — The AI Tool Use Case request form, countersigned by the Department Head, is the foundational record of the business justification.

2. Assessment documentation (Steps 4–5) — The data identification and DPIA (where applicable) and the formal risk assessment are produced and retained as assessment records.

3. Control schedule (Step 6) — The control identification record, including all selected controls and their implementation tasks, is saved and version-controlled.

4. Verification evidence (Step 7) — Control verification testing results and operational control activation records are retained as evidence of pre-approval testing.

5. Central inventory registration (Step 11) — AI Governance Team registers the approved use case in the central inventory. All authorisation records, assessments, Board decisions, and operational controls documentation are retained. technology risk assessments and DPIAs are held separately.

6. Ongoing review records (Step 12) — Periodic review outcomes and triggered review reports are added to the retained record, maintaining a complete lifecycle audit trail.
jkObjective: The AI governance workflow (Steps 2–12) generates a complete set of records at each stage, retained in the central inventory under Step 11, constituting the organisation's record-keeping system under ISO 18286.8.
jkImplementationEvidence: Step 14 central inventory registration record, containing all linked authorisation artefacts: request form, tool evaluation, risk assessment, DPIA, control schedule, verification report, and Board decision.

jkName: AI Governance Workflow — Instructions for Use Compliance
jkText:
Conformity with ISO 42001.5 is maintained through Steps 2 and 10 of this governance workflow, which establish and communicate the boundaries within which the AI system must be operated:

1. Intended purpose boundary (Step 2) — The AI Tool Use Case request form defines the approved scope of use. The organisation operates the system only within the intended purpose documented in this form, which serves as the internal instructions for use.

2. User obligations briefing (Step 10) — Before access is granted, authorised users receive a use-case-specific briefing that defines exactly what they are responsible for and what the system is responsible for. Users are explicitly informed of the approved scope and prohibited inputs.

3. Controls enforcement (Step 7) — Operational controls confirmed active prior to user access — including data filtering, output review checkpoints, and disclosure labelling — enforce the usage boundaries set in Step 2 at a technical level.

4. Ongoing compliance (Step 12) — Periodic reviews confirm that actual usage remains consistent with the documented intended purpose. Any drift from the approved scope triggers a re-assessment.
jkObjective: Steps 2 and 10 of the AI governance workflow ensure the system is operated strictly within its declared intended purpose and in accordance with the usage boundaries set during authorisation, satisfying the deployer compliance obligation of ISO 42001.5.
jkImplementationEvidence: Saved Step 2 request form (scope and intended purpose), Step 13 user obligations briefing record, and Step 12 operational controls activation confirmation.

jkName: AI Governance Workflow — Design and Development Controls
jkText:
Conformity with ISO 18286.3 is maintained through Steps 5 and 6 of this governance workflow, which together constitute the organisation's design control and verification process:

1. Risk identification and scoping (Step 5) — The formal risk assessment identifies and evaluates all legal, regulatory, and EU AI Act obligations applicable to the use case, informed by the data identification and DPIA data inventory (Step 4). This constitutes the hazard analysis phase of a design control process.

2. Control design (Step 6) — The risk team selects specific, verifiable controls to mitigate each identified risk. Controls must be concrete and implementable — not delegated to user judgement. This is the design phase.

3. Compliance verification (Step 6, AI Act Compliance Controls view) — The compliance team independently verifies that every applicable harmonised standard requirement has at least one selected control, surfacing uncovered requirements as gaps. This is the verification phase.

4. Design review gate (Step 8) — The AI Change Board reviews the complete design package before any implementation proceeds, providing an independent design review gate with a documented approval record.

5. Implementation verification (Step 7) — All controls defined in Step 6 must be confirmed active before user access is granted, completing the design-to-implementation verification cycle.
jkObjective: Steps 5 and 6 of the AI governance workflow, combined with the Step 8 Board gate and Step 7 controls verification, constitute the organisation's design and development control process under ISO 18286.3.
jkImplementationEvidence: Saved Step 8 risk assessment, Step 9 control schedule with zero unresolved HS gaps, Step 11 Board approval record, and Step 12 controls activation confirmation.

jkText:
Conformity with ISO 18286.4 is maintained through the resource prerequisites and specialist functions embedded in this governance workflow:

1. Training prerequisite (Step 1) — No use case may proceed without the requestor confirming current AI risk awareness training, ensuring the minimum human competence standard is met before any AI tool is accessed.

2. Specialist risk assessment (Step 5) — The formal risk assessment is conducted by the AI Governance Team, applying specialist knowledge to assess domain reliability, bias characteristics, and vendor risks for each use case.

3. DPO resource (Step 4) — Where personal data is involved, the DPO leads the DPIA, ensuring qualified data protection expertise is applied before any deployment proceeds.

4. AI Governance Team risk and control function (Steps 5–6) — Risk identification and control selection conducted by the AI Governance Team ensure that qualified risk management resources are applied to each use case at the due diligence stage.

5. AI Change Board (Step 8) — The Board constitutes a standing expert governance body with the technical and legal competence to evaluate the complete authorisation package.

6. User obligations briefing (Step 10) — Role-specific briefings ensure authorised users have the knowledge required to discharge their specific obligations within the approved use case.
jkObjective: The AI governance workflow embeds resource management under ISO 18286.4 through mandatory competence prerequisites, specialist function assignments, and targeted user briefings at each stage.
jkImplementationEvidence: Step 1 training confirmation, Step 6 tool fitness evaluation (conducted by AI Governance Team/AI Working Group), Step 11 Board review record, and Step 13 user obligations briefing acknowledgement.

jkText:
Conformity with ISO 18286.5 is maintained through Step 12 of this governance workflow, which constitutes the organisation's post-market monitoring system:

1. Risk-proportionate review schedule (Step 12) — Each approved AI tool use case undergoes periodic reviews at a frequency set by the AI Governance Team based on the risk level assigned during authorisation. Higher-risk tools are reviewed more frequently.

2. Performance monitoring scope (Step 12) — Periodic reviews confirm that the business case remains valid, the risk assessment is current, and operational controls remain active, including after any vendor model updates.

3. Triggered review mechanism (Step 12) — Immediate reviews are initiated following security incidents, vendor model changes, regulatory updates, or significant organisational changes. Model changes trigger a re-assessment — the risk assessment (Step 5) and controls (Step 6) are reviewed before continued use is permitted.

4. Feedback loop (Step 12) — Review trends are escalated to AI Governance Team for targeted training updates under AI SR7, and Steering Committee receives ongoing governance reports.

5. Re-assessment pathway — Where a review identifies material risk changes or control failures, the workflow can be re-entered at the appropriate step to produce updated assessments and revised Board authorisation.
jkObjective: Step 12 of the AI governance workflow constitutes the organisation's post-market monitoring system under ISO 18286.5, providing risk-proportionate periodic reviews and event-triggered re-assessments across the full lifecycle of each approved AI use case.
jkImplementationEvidence: Step 15 review schedule and completed review records for the use case, including any triggered review reports following incidents or vendor model changes.

jkText:
Conformity with ISO 18286.6 is maintained through the triggered review mechanism in Step 12 and the AI Governance Team escalation framework:

1. Incident detection (Steps 7, 10, 12) — Output logging and anomaly flagging confirmed active in Step 7, user reporting obligations briefed in Step 10, and the triggered review mechanism in Step 12 form a three-layer incident detection capability.

2. Triggered review activation (Step 12) — Any security incident or breach related to AI tool usage initiates an immediate triggered review. The review updates the risk and control self-assessment, assesses control adequacy, and produces a documented incident report.

3. AI Governance Team escalation — The AI Governance Team is the responsible function for assessing whether an incident constitutes a serious incident requiring notification to a national supervisory authority under the EU AI Act. The CISO holds sign-off on external notification decisions.

4. User reporting channel (Step 10) — Authorised users are obligated to report anomalous, harmful, or unexpected outputs to AI Governance Team, providing a front-line incident detection path.

5. Record retention (Step 11) — All triggered review reports and incident records are retained in the central inventory as part of the post-market monitoring record.
jkObjective: Steps 7, 10, and 12 of the AI governance workflow, combined with the AI Governance Team escalation framework, constitute the organisation's incident detection, response, and reporting procedures under ISO 18286.6.
jkImplementationEvidence: Step 15 triggered review report (where applicable), AI Governance Team incident escalation record, and Step 14 retained incident documentation.

jkText:
Conformity with ISO 18286.7 is maintained through the documentation produced and retained by this governance workflow, which constitutes the Technical File required by Article 11:

1. System description (Step 2) — The AI Tool Use Case request form documents the system name, intended purpose, and operational scope.

2. Risk assessment and control schedule (Steps 5–6) — The formal risk assessment and control schedule document the identified risks, applicable EU AI Act obligations, and the specific controls selected to address them.

3. Data documentation (Step 4) — The data identification records and DPIA (where applicable) document the data types processed, lawful basis, and data governance arrangements.

4. Testing evidence (Step 7) — Control verification testing and operational control activation results document the performance evidence and validation outcomes.

5. Conformity assessment record (Step 8 report) — The AI Change Board approval package and the conformity report constitute the formal technical file, including system description, applicable articles, harmonised standard requirement coverage, and end-to-end control traceability.

6. Retention (Step 11) — All technical documentation is registered in the central inventory and retained for the applicable period.
jkObjective: The AI governance workflow produces and retains the complete set of technical documentation required by ISO 18286.7 and Article 11, with the Step 8 conformity report serving as the primary Technical File document.
jkImplementationEvidence: Step 11 conformity report, Step 14 central inventory registration record, and the complete linked documentation package retained for the use case.

jkText: The CISO maintains a documented AI tool oversight and monitoring plan that defines what aspects of AI tool usage are monitored, the monitoring frequency, the metrics and thresholds applied, and the roles responsible. The plan is reviewed and updated as the AI tool estate and risk profile change.
jkObjective: Establish a CISO-owned plan defining the scope, cadence and ownership of AI tool usage monitoring.
jkImplementationEvidence: The current AI tool oversight and monitoring plan, reviewed at each periodic review (Step 12), with the control's status recorded and monitored in Riskonnect under the risk and control self-assessment.

jkText: The AI Governance Team collects usage data across all authorised AI tools — access events, request volumes, user populations, and data-classification flags — into a central monitoring view available to the CISO. Collection runs continuously and feeds the periodic and triggered reviews.
jkObjective: Provide the CISO with systematic, ongoing visibility of AI tool usage as the basis for oversight.
jkImplementationEvidence: Usage-monitoring records reviewed at each periodic review (Step 12), with the control's status recorded and monitored in Riskonnect under the risk and control self-assessment.

jkText: Monitoring of AI tool usage includes detection of drift and anomalies — material shifts in usage volume, user population, data classification handled, or tool behaviour — that may signal emerging risk between scheduled reviews. Detected anomalies are flagged to the CISO and can initiate a triggered review.
jkObjective: Detect material changes in AI tool usage between formal reviews so emerging risk is surfaced early.
jkImplementationEvidence: Anomaly and drift detection outputs reviewed at periodic and triggered reviews (Step 12), with the control's status recorded and monitored in Riskonnect under the risk and control self-assessment.

jkText: A defined channel routes AI tool incidents, issues and user-reported concerns to the CISO and the risk function for assessment. The channel is communicated to authorised users and feeds the triggered-review process where a security incident or breach related to AI tool usage occurs.
jkObjective: Provide a defined escalation path for AI tool incidents into CISO oversight and triggered review.
jkImplementationEvidence: Incident and escalation records and any resulting triggered reviews (Step 12), with the control's status recorded and monitored in Riskonnect under the risk and control self-assessment.

jkName: Corrective Action & risk and control self-assessment Update
jkText: Findings from AI tool usage monitoring — anomalies, incidents, control failures or recurring issues — are translated into corrective actions, and the status of the affected controls is updated in the risk and control self-assessment. Recurring issues also feed targeted awareness and training under AI SR7.
jkObjective: Close the loop from monitoring findings to corrective action and updated risk and control self-assessment control status.
jkImplementationEvidence: Corrective action records and updated risk and control self-assessment control status in Riskonnect, evidenced through periodic and triggered review outputs (Step 12).
